description: Use SIMD shuffle-based lookup tables (PSHUFB/TBL) to classify every byte in a 16/32/64-byte chunk into one of several categories (delimiter, quote, newline, whitespace, other) in a single instruction, replacing multi-branch switch statements. This technique from simdjson's vectorized classification can handle CSV's smaller alphabet even more efficiently, producing per-category bitmasks in 2-3 SIMD instructions.
mathematical_formalization: Define classification function f: byte -> {COMMA, QUOTE, NEWLINE, CR, OTHER}. Implement as: low_nibble = byte & 0x0F, high_nibble = byte >> 4. class = LUT_low[low_nibble] & LUT_high[high_nibble]. LUT_low and LUT_high are 16-byte SIMD registers used with PSHUFB. The AND combines the two 4-bit lookups into exact classification. 2 PSHUFB + 1 AND per 16 bytes = 0.1875 instructions/byte.
analogical_connections: Perfect hashing: the nibble-split lookup is a form of perfect hash function for a small character set, similar to minimal perfect hashing in compiler symbol tables
FPGA look-up tables: the PSHUFB approach mirrors how FPGAs implement arbitrary boolean functions via LUTs, just in software
Bloom filter probing: the two-table AND-combination resembles a 2-hash Bloom filter check
implementation_hypothesis: For CSV, we only need to detect 4 characters: comma (0x2C), quote (0x22), LF (0x0A), CR (0x0D). Construct two 16-byte LUTs where LUT_low[nibble] has bits set for characters sharing that low nibble, LUT_high[nibble] has bits set for characters sharing that high nibble. AND the results to get exact matches. Extract per-class bitmasks with additional SIMD comparisons or bit manipulation.
experiment_seed: Benchmark vectorized classification vs. scalar switch-case on random byte streams and real CSV data. Measure instructions per byte, branch mispredictions (should be ~0 for vectorized). Compare PSHUFB (SSE), VPSHUFB (AVX2), VPERMB (AVX-512), and TBL (NEON) implementations.
